title: On the Incarnation
subtitle: De Incarnatione Verbi Dei
source: Translation: A Religious of CSMV, 1944 / earlier NPNF II.4 (1892). Public domain.

sections.title: The Word and Creation
paragraphs: In our former book we dealt fully enough with a few of the chief points about the heathen worship of idols, and how those false fears originally arose. We also, by God's grace, briefly indicated that the Word of the Father is Himself divine, that all things that are owe their being to His will and power, and that it is through Him that the Father gives order to creation, by Him that all things are moved, and through Him that they receive their being.

Now, Macarius, true lover of Christ, we must take a step further in the faith of our holy religion, and consider also the Word's becoming Man and His divine Appearing in our midst. That mystery the Jews traduce, the Greeks deride, but we adore; and your own love and devotion to the Word also will be the greater, because in His Manhood He seems so little worth.

For it is the custom of men, who have set their love on things invisible and transcending sense, when they have learned that a thing has lost the dignity that once it had, to bestow on it the more honor and affection.
notes: Athanasius opens by referring to his earlier work, Contra Gentes; the two together form a paired apologetic.
'Macarius' is the addressee; nothing certain is known of him beyond that he was a catechumen.

sections.title: Why the Word Became Man
paragraphs: You must understand why it is that the Word of the Father, so great and so high, has been made manifest in bodily form. He has not assumed a body as proper to His own nature, far from it, for as the Word He is without body. He has been manifested in a human body for this reason only, out of the love and goodness of His Father, for the salvation of us men.

We will begin, then, with the creation of the world and with God its Maker, for the first fact that you must grasp is this: the renewal of creation has been the work of the self-same Word that made it at the beginning. There is thus no inconsistency between creation and salvation; for the One Father has employed the same Agent for both works, effecting the salvation of the world through the same Word who made it in the beginning.
notes: The phrase 'love and goodness of His Father' anchors the work in divine philanthropia, the central category of Eastern soteriology.

sections.title: He Became What We Are
paragraphs: The Word of God came in His own Person, because it was He alone, the Image of the Father, Who could recreate man made after the Image. In order to effect this re-creation, however, He had first to do away with death and corruption. Therefore He assumed a human body, in order that in it death might once for all be destroyed, and that men might be renewed according to the Image.

For this reason, then, He assumed a body capable of death, in order that, by partaking of the Word who is above all, it might be sufficient for death on behalf of all, and through the indwelling Word might remain incorruptible, and that thenceforth corruption might cease from all by the grace of the Resurrection. He, the Mighty One, the Artificer of all, prepared the body in the Virgin as a temple for Himself, and made it His very own as an instrument, in it manifested and in it dwelling.
notes: This passage contains the formula often paraphrased: 'He became man that we might become god.' The doctrine of theosis flows from it.
